title: Empty homes in City-funded supportive housing
question: How many permanent supportive housing units in buildings the City funds stand empty, how many are offline rather than being filled, and what does an empty unit cost?
finding: On the dashboard updated 11/12/2026, 761 of 9,198 site-based units were vacant (8.3%, against the department's own 7% target): 90 available for referral, 308 with a move-in in progress and 363 offline. Over the twelve months from 2025-12 to 2026-11 vacancies averaged 778 a month (373 offline, 406 being filled) and never fell below 744; offline units went from 414 in 2025-12 to 363 in 2026-11 (low 329), while units being filled rose from 340 to a peak of 450. Largest offline reasons: janitorial maintenance 77, property hold 68, internal transfer 59. The excess over the 7% target is about 117 units. At the homelessness department's own pre-purchase estimate of $19,800 a unit a year for operations and services, an average of 373 offline units is about $7,385,400 a year of budgeted operating cost; at the $30,047 later estimated for one site, $11,207,531. A new building in lease-up, Harbor Haven, had 22 of 67 counted units empty (expected 125 units), outside these counts.
how: Read from the owner's prints of the department's Power BI dashboard (two pages; a third print repeats page two). Monthly totals were read column by column from the chart; each month's total equals the two parts, the twelve-month averages equal those printed (778, 406, 373) and the last month equals the page-one counts, which identifies the parts as online and offline. The cost yardstick multiplies offline units by per-unit operating figures from Budget and Legislative Analyst reports on Files 220133 ($19,800, the department's budgeted maximum for a Homekey building) and 220885 ($30,047, the revised estimate for 3055-3061 16th Street).
limits: The dashboard gives counts on a date, not how long each unit has been empty, so no unit can be said to have been empty for months; the department's unit-level vacancy records would. Some vacancy is unavoidable (turnover, repairs, a death in a unit); the department's own target is 7%. An empty unit does not cost its full operating budget (services are partly per resident, and some leases are paid per occupied unit), so the cost figure is a yardstick, not a loss. The sf.gov housing inventory prints carry the page text only: the inventory dashboard printed blank, so the number of units by program is not on disk. The department says June 2023 and March 2024 data are unavailable because of system changes. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
